Title: Fix Initial Codes and Iteratively Refine Textual Directions Toward Safe Multi-Turn Code Correction
Text:

Fix Initial Codes and Iteratively Refine Textual Directions
Toward Safe Multi-Turn Code Correction
Yuto Tanaka & Issei Sato
Department of Computer Science
The University of Tokyo
Tokyo, Japan

Abstract
Recent work on large language models (LLMs) has emphasized the im-
portance of scaling inference compute. From this perspective, the state-
of-the-art method SCATTERED FOREST SEARCH (SFS) has been proposed,
employing Monte Carlo Tree Search with carefully crafted initial seeds and
textual optimization for multi-turn code correction. However, its complex-
ity makes it unclear what factors contribute to improvements in inference
performance. To address this problem, we analyze SFS and propose a sim-
pler method, ITERATIVE REFINEMENT OF TEXTUAL DIRECTIONS (IRTD),
which fixes initial codes and iteratively refines textual directions. Because
of the simplicity of IRTD, we theoretically establish the safety of IRTD using
Oracle-Guided Inductive Synthesis (OGIS). Experiments on several code
generation benchmarks suggest that IRTD achieves inference performance
comparable to state-of-the-art methods. These results indicate that, even
without complex search structures, refining initial codes with high-quality
textual directions alone can effectively improve inference performance.
1
Introduction
Recent work on large language models (LLMs) has increasingly focused on scaling inference-
time compute to improve inference performance (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024). In
such approaches, the goal is to obtain higher-quality outputs by expanding the computa-
tional process at inference time, without modifying the model’s parameters or the training
data. Thus, this paradigm is collectively referred to as inference scaling. Several represen-
tative approaches have been proposed under this paradigm, including best-of-N (BoN)
sampling (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al., 2023), linear self-refinement methods (Madaan
et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023), and tree-search-based methods that integrate multiple reason-
ing trajectories (Tian et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024).
A representative task in the study of inference scaling is code generation. In this context,
multi-turn code correction, in which an initial program is refined through multiple rounds
of feedback, has been widely studied as a practical approach to improving output quality.
Previous methods such as BoN and iterative refinement have been shown to improve
performance (Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024). One reason for this effectiveness is that
providing enough trials increases the probability that an LLM will sample a correct answer
(Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024). However, Light et al. (2025) have shown that existing
methods often generate highly similar outputs, resulting in insufficient exploration of the
solution space.
Light et al. (2025) have proposed SCATTERED FOREST SEARCH (SFS) that builds on Monte
Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) and incorporates techniques such as careful seed initialization
and textual optimization. They have empirically reported that SFS achieves state-of-the-
art performance in multi-turn code correction (Light et al., 2025). However, since SFS
tightly integrates multiple components, it is unclear what factors drive improvements in
inference performance. This ambiguity hinders the development of simpler and more

efficient approaches that could retain the benefits of inference scaling without relying on
costly or complex search mechanisms.
To address the problem, we analyze SFS to identify the essential factors that contribute to
performance improvements. In these analyses, we reveal that breadth-wise exploration
toward high-quality textual directions plays a crucial role in the self-refinement process.
From this finding, we propose ITERATIVE REFINEMENT OF TEXTUAL DIRECTIONS that fixes
initial codes and iteratively refines textual directions. IRTD is a simpler method than SFS for
multi-turn code correction and is capable of achieving comparable inference performance.
Moreover, because of its simplicity, we theoretically establish the safety of IRTD using
the framework of Oracle-Guided Inductive Synthesis (OGIS) (Jha & Seshia, 2017a;b). This
theoretical analysis ensures that IRTD does not lose the true solution and can reach the
correct answer.
In summary, our main contributions include:
• We analyze SFS and reveal that breadth-wise exploration is more important than
depth-wise exploration for multi-turn code correction.
• We propose a simpler method, IRTD, which iteratively revises textual directions
while fixing initial codes as the target codes.
• We theoretically analyze IRTD based on the framework of OGIS and show the safety
of IRTD as a multi-turn code correction method. This guarantees that IRTD does
not lose the true solution in the refinement process.
• We empirically evaluate IRTD on several code generation benchmarks and confirm
that IRTD achieves performance comparable to SFS.
2
Related work
Recent studies have increasingly focused on improving model performance by allocating
more computation at inference time (Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024). One of the simplest
and most common methods is best-of-N (BoN) sampling (Cobbe et al., 2021; Lightman et al.,
2023). In this approach, multiple samples are generated from the same prompt to ensure
diversity among responses and improve output quality. Prior work has also proposed self-
correction methods in which an initial response is generated and then iteratively verified
and revised (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). These methods improve the model’s
responses by incorporating internal or external feedback as additional information. Yang
et al. (2025) has proposed a probabilistic theory of self-correction to explain the performance
improvements observed in these methods.
Furthermore, incorporating tree search methods such as DFS, BFS, and MCTS has been
shown to be effective for inference scaling. Prior work has applied tree search to multi-step
tasks, including selecting the next reasoning step in reasoning processes (Yao et al., 2023;
Besta et al., 2024; Tian et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024) and decoding the next token during
generation (Feng et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023). Tree search has also been applied to
optimization problems, where it functions as a black-box method for exploring a solution
space (Light et al., 2025).
Overall, we build upon previous research (Light et al., 2025) and aim to identify the factors
that truly contribute to performance improvements in increasingly complex inference scaling
methods. Motivated by these observations, our study proposes a simpler method and
demonstrates that performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods can be achieved
without relying on complex search strategies.
3
Understanding SCATTERED FOREST SEARCH (SFS)
This section provides an overview of SFS, which is a state-of-the-art method for multi-turn
code correction, and presents analyses of SFS.

3.1
Problem formulation
Following Light et al. (2025), we formulate code generation as a black-box optimization
problem (Golovin et al., 2017). A code generation task is represented as x = ⟨p, H⟩, where p
denotes a prompt written in natural language or code, and H represents a set of hidden test
cases used for evaluation. The objective is to provide an LLM with a prompt p and generate
a code c ∼LLM(p) that passes all hidden tests in H. Although the model cannot access
the hidden tests, it can generate a set of validation tests V. Using these validation tests
V and the program execution environment, the model obtains feedback on its generated
code c. This feedback is then used to determine whether the code should be refined. In the
evaluation phase, generated codes are evaluated against a hidden test set H and are deemed
correct only when all tests are passed. For each task, an LLM is allowed to generate codes up
to k times, and a task is considered solved if at least one of them is correct. Following these
rules, for a task set X, the evaluation metric Pass@k Rate (Chen et al., 2021) is calculated as
the proportion of tasks x ∈X that are solved with at most k generated codes. An overview
of this problem formulation is illustrated in Appendix A.
3.2
SCATTERED FOREST SEARCH (SFS)
Several inference-time methods have been explored in prior work to improve LLM perfor-
mance on code generation tasks. However, Light et al. (2025) have shown that these methods
often generate highly similar candidate codes, resulting in insufficient exploration of the
solution space. To address this challenge, they have also proposed SCATTERED FOREST
SEARCH (SFS) (Light et al., 2025). SFS is a MCTS-based method that combines careful seed
initialization with textual optimization and consists of the following three components.
• SCATTERING: Dynamically varies input prompts with different textual directions
when sampling revised codes.
• FORESTING: Generates multiple initial codes that act as starting points for MCTS.
• SCOUTING: Provides feedback on textual directions employed during the refine-
ment process and distills general insights that can be shared across search branches.
Their study has confirmed that SFS outperforms existing methods in terms of inference
scaling performance (Light et al., 2025). Details of SFS are provided in Appendix B.
3.3
Theoretical and empirical analysis of SFS
Theoretical analysis. In SFS, Algorithm 1 is used to select a code for revision. The loop
condition holds only when the current node has a better child node on the validation tests
and there are no unused textual directions remaining. As long as this condition is not
satisfied, exploration in the depth direction does not proceed. Under this condition, we
have the following theorem.
Theorem 1. Assume that the root has no remaining unexpanded actions and that there exists at
least one better child. In the initial phase, if there are few depth-1 nodes that have no unexpanded
actions and possess a better child, or if the root-level UCT does not strongly concentrate on such child
nodes, the selection process is likely to terminate at depth 1 with high probability, and the probability
of reaching depth 2 is low.

The proof of Theorem 1 is provided in Appendix C.1. This theorem indicates that when the
number of refinement steps is relatively small (around a dozen), the expansion of revised
codes tends to be biased toward the breadth direction rather than the depth direction.
Empirical analysis. We analyzed the search trees produced by SFS and NO FORESTING,
which removes FORESTING component from SFS. We used gpt-4o-mini as the base model
in three datasets: HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) and APPS
(Hendrycks et al., 2021). For both methods, we set the number of codes generated per task
at k = 16. Following the original paper, we configured SFS to generate 5 initial codes and
perform up to 11 revision steps, while we configured NO FORESTING to generate 1 initial
code and perform up to 15 revision steps.
For problems where a correct code is found, we analyzed the distribution of the depth at
which the first correct code appears in the search tree. The results in Table 1 suggest that,
in almost all cases, the first correct code appears among the initial codes or after a single
refinement of them. Furthermore, as shown in Table 2, a similar trend is observed even in
NO FORESTING, which generates only a single initial code. These observations indicate
that deep-wise exploration contributes little to reaching correct codes, while breadth-wise
exploration that yields high-quality textual directions plays a more important role in the
refinement process. Further analyses are provided in Appendix C.2.

4
ITERATIVE REFINEMENT OF TEXTUAL DIRECTIONS (IRTD)
From the findings in Section 3.3, we hypothesize that if textual directions are of high quality,
refining initial codes may become effective in multi-turn code correction. Accordingly, we
propose ITERATIVE REFINEMENT OF TEXTUAL DIRECTIONS (IRTD), which refines initial
codes through iterative feedback on textual directions.
• Section 4.1 presents the framework of IRTD, which becomes simpler than SFS.
• Section 4.2 theoretically analyzes IRTD based on the framework of Oracle-Guided
Inductive Synthesis (OGIS) (Jha & Seshia, 2017a;b).
4.1
Proposed framework
Given an input prompt, IRTD first generates one or multiple initial codes. It then generates
one or more textual directions for the selected initial code and uses one of them to refine
the code. After this refinement step, it evaluates the refined code on the validation tests
and provides feedback on the used textual direction, which is stored as shared information.
This shared information is then used as an additional context for an LLM when generating
textual directions in subsequent refinement steps. IRTD repeats this refinement process
iteratively until a desired condition is met. In contrast to existing self-refinement methods,
IRTD fixes the initial codes as the refinement targets throughout the process. Moreover, by giving
feedback on textual directions, IRTD enhances the probability of successful refinements. An
overview of IRTD is illustrated in Appendix D. Next, we describe IRTD in detail under the
problem formulation introduced in Section 3.1.

4.2
Theoretical analysis using Oracle-Guided Inductive Synthesis (OGIS)
We show the safety of IRTD using the framework of OGIS (Jha & Seshia, 2017a;b). In
OGIS, program safety is defined by the absence of counterexamples found by an oracle (a
formal verifier). Building on this, the following three properties regarding the version space
are required to guarantee that an inductive algorithm interacting with the oracle reliably
converges to a safe program.
• The version space shrinks monotonically with each step by eliminating incorrect
hypotheses that contradict the counterexamples provided by the oracle.
• As a premise for the search, the target hypothesis is assumed to exist within the
initial hypothesis space.
• Since the target hypothesis does not contradict any counterexample, it is never
eliminated from the version space.
By satisfying these properties, it is shown that the algorithm can reliably synthesize a safe
program in a finite number of steps. Therefore, it is important to theoretically demonstrate
the safety of the method in multi-turn code correction.

5
Experiments
We numerically evaluated IRTD on several code generation benchmarks.
• Section 5.1 describes the experimental setup.
• Section 5.2 reports the inference performance of IRTD compared to baseline methods.
Although IRTD is a simpler method than SFS, it achieves comparable performance.
• Section 5.3 reports the diversity of textual directions in IRTD. As the number of
initial codes increases, the diversity of textual directions tends to grow.
5.1
Experimental setup
We used gpt-4o-mini as the base model and evaluated IRTD on several code generation
benchmarks, including HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and
APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021). We compared IRTD with various existing baselines, setting
the number of codes generated per task at k = 16 for all methods. The detailed settings of
all evaluated methods are provided in Table 3.

5.2
Inference scaling
We compared the inference scaling behavior of IRTD with that of existing methods. Figure 1
shows the results for APPS. The results for the other datasets are reported in Appendix F.1.
Each curve represents the mean performance over five runs, and each shaded region denotes
95% confidence intervals computed using the t-distribution. We found that IRTD achieves
inference scaling performance comparable to or better than that of prior methods. Notably,
although our method is simpler, it attains inference performance on par with SFS, which is
among state-of-the-art methods.
5.3
Diversity of textual directions
To quantify diversity in IRTD, we measured the average cosine similarity between the
generated textual directions across different refinement steps. We used the ‘all-MiniLM-L6-
v2’ model of SentenceTransformers (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019) to obtain embeddings for
these textual directions and summarized our results as heatmaps. Figure 2 shows the results
for APPS. The results for the other datasets are included in Appendix F.2. We observed
that increasing the number of initial codes leads to greater diversity in textual directions.
This suggests that increasing the number of initial codes enables IRTD to generate textual
directions that are not achievable with fewer initial codes, which is consistent with our
theoretical analysis on discriminative power.

6
Conclusion
We have analyzed the state-of-the-art method SFS and found that breadth-wise exploration
toward high-quality textual directions plays an important role in the self-refinement process.
From this analysis, we propose IRTD as a simpler method for multi-turn code correction.
The simplicity of IRTD enables theoretical analysis, allowing us to provide guarantees on
the safety of the method. Experimental results demonstrate that IRTD achieves competitive
performance compared to SFS without requiring complex search structures. These findings
provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying improved inference performance in
multi-turn code correction and suggest promising directions for future research.

B
Details of SCATTERED FOREST SEARCH (SFS)
To enable diverse exploration of the solution space in code generation, Light et al. (2025)
have proposed SCATTERED FOREST SEARCH (SFS). SFS builds on MCTS and incorporates
techniques such as careful seed initialization and textual optimization. This method encour-
ages broader exploration of the solution space by combining LLM-driven textual directions,
the introduction of multiple initial codes, and the utilization of feedback and past search
experience. Specifically, SFS consists of three main components: SCATTERING, FORESTING,
and SCOUTING, as illustrated in Figure 4.
SCATTERING: This component dynamically varies input prompts with different textual
directions when sampling revised codes. More concretely, given a code selected by MCTS

FORESTING: This component generates multiple initial codes that act as starting points
for MCTS. In this process, initial codes are generated using either the same base prompt or
diversified prompts obtained by randomly appending instruction statements.
SCOUTING: This component provides feedback on the textual directions used during the
refinement process and distills general insights that can be shared across search branches.
These insights are incorporated into the prompt as auxiliary information when an LLM
generates reflections and textual directions. This enables the promotion of effective textual
directions and the suppression of unproductive ones.

E.1
Conceptual origin of version space
The notion of version space originates as a fundamental concept in learning theory, where
it denotes the set of hypotheses that are consistent with the observed data. In learning
theory, let H denotes the hypothesis space, and let D = {(x1, y1) , . . . , (xn, yn)} denotes the
observed (training) data. Then, the version space is defined as
VSH(D) := {h ∈H | h (xi) = yi for all i} .
(26)
From the perspective of version space, learning can be viewed as a process of progressively
eliminating hypotheses based on the training data.

Abstract: Recent work on large language models (LLMs) has emphasized the im- portance of scaling inference compute. From this perspective, the state- of-the-art method SCATTERED FOREST SEARCH (SFS) has been proposed, employing Monte Carlo Tree Search with carefully crafted initial seeds and textual optimization for multi-turn code correction. However, its complex- ity makes it unclear what factors contribute to improvements in inference performance. To address this problem, we analyze SFS and propose a sim- pler method, ITERATIVE REFINEMENT OF TEXTUAL DIRECTIONS (IRTD), which fixes initial codes and iteratively refines textual directions. Because of the simplicity of IRTD, we theoretically establish the safety of IRTD using Oracle-Guided Inductive Synthesis (OGIS). Experiments on several code generation benchmarks suggest that IRTD achieves inference performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods. These results indicate that, even without complex search structures, refining initial codes with high-quality textual directions alone can effectively improve inference performance.
